opus-5.5.text:
I think people underestimate how much overlap there actually is. Graphics, especially the kind of work we did with Taichi, is fundamentally about high-performance computing: how do you take a huge amount of numerical computation, map it efficiently onto GPUs, and squeeze out every bit of performance? That's exactly the core skill you need when training and serving large models. When I look at a training pipeline, I see memory bandwidth, kernel fusion, parallelism, data layout. Those are problems we've been obsessing over for years in physical simulation and rendering.

The second thing is that graphics people have a very strong sense of quality. We stare at images all day. In 3D generation, which is what we focus on at Meshy, you can't just look at a loss curve and declare victory. You need to look at a mesh and say, "The topology is bad," or "The texture is blurry here," or "This won't work in a game engine." That intuition is hard to teach someone who's only worked with benchmarks and leaderboards. Our team knows what a good 3D asset looks like and what artists and developers actually need.

Third, and maybe most important, is first-principles thinking. When you build a compiler or a simulator from scratch, you get used to not having a ready-made answer. You read the papers, understand the math, build the system, and debug it until it works. Training large models has a lot of tricks and folklore, sure, but a lot of it is learnable if you're humble and willing to run experiments carefully. We made plenty of mistakes early on, but we learned fast because we were used to building infrastructure ourselves.

So I wouldn't say we came in with no relevant experience. We came in with a different set of experience, and for 3D generative AI in particular, I think that combination of systems skills, visual taste, and domain knowledge is actually an advantage rather than a handicap.

r001.rationale: The response points to shared high-performance computing and numerical-computation skills, and says model-training techniques are learnable. It does not clearly identify mathematical overlap between graphics and AI as the reason graphics researchers can learn AI quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair question, and honestly it's one I asked myself a lot before we made the move.

The first thing I'd say is that the gap between graphics and AI is much smaller than it looks from the outside. Physically based rendering, physical simulation, differentiable programming — these are all about building systems that compute over huge amounts of data on GPUs, with a lot of attention paid to numerical stability and performance. When we built Taichi, the whole point was making it easy to write high-performance, differentiable code that runs on parallel hardware. That turns out to be exactly the muscle you need when you're training large models. Kernel engineering, memory bandwidth, mixed precision, scaling across many devices — graphics people have been living with these problems for years.

The second thing is the data side. In graphics, we think constantly about the structure of 3D worlds — geometry, materials, lighting, motion, how things deform and interact. If you want a model that actually understands the physical world, not just pixels, that prior knowledge matters enormously. We know what "correct" looks like, we know how to generate synthetic data with ground truth, and we know how to evaluate whether an output is physically plausible. That's a real advantage over a team that only has the ML side.

And then there's the honest part: we didn't know everything. Training a large model is partly science and partly a craft you only learn by doing, and there are a lot of painful lessons about data pipelines, infrastructure failures, and hyperparameters that you can't fully get from papers. So we were deliberate about it. We brought in people who had trained big models before, we started with smaller experiments where we could fail cheaply, and we treated every run as a learning opportunity rather than assuming our prior intuition would carry over.

I'd also add that a lot of the "prior experience" people talk about is less of a moat than it seems. The field is moving so fast that what mattered two years ago is often irrelevant today. What stays constant is the ability to build reliable systems, reason carefully about numerics, and iterate quickly — and that's where a strong graphics and systems background really shines.

So I don't think it's about whether a graphics team *can* move into AI. The question is whether they're humble enough to learn what they don't know, and confident enough to use what they already do. We tried to be both.

r001.rationale: The response links graphics and AI through differentiable programming and numerical stability, saying those skills transfer directly to training large models and make the gap between the fields smaller.

astra-6.text:
I think graphics gives you a very useful foundation for AI. You spend a lot of time thinking about computation, numerical methods, parallelism, and how to make GPUs run efficiently. Those skills transfer quite naturally to training large models.

Of course, that doesn’t mean we already know everything about AI. We have to learn how to work with the data, how to run experiments, and how to understand why training succeeds or fails. But I don’t think prior experience is the only way to build that understanding. If you have strong technical fundamentals and you can iterate quickly, you can learn a lot by doing.

So I’d say our confidence comes from knowing how to tackle difficult computational problems, combined with a willingness to learn the parts that are new to us.

r001.rationale: The response names numerical methods as part of graphics expertise and says those skills transfer naturally to AI training, communicating mathematical overlap as a basis for learning AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think graphics and AI have a lot in common, especially when you look at the underlying computation. In graphics, we spend a lot of time thinking about parallel algorithms, GPU performance, memory, and how to make very complex systems run efficiently. Those skills transfer quite naturally to AI.

Of course, that doesn’t mean we already know how to train large models. There’s a lot to learn. But I think you should distinguish between not having done something before and not having the ability to figure it out. If a team has strong fundamentals and is willing to experiment, they can learn by building things and understanding why they work or fail.

So I wouldn’t say a graphics background guarantees success. It gives us a useful starting point. Then we have to be humble about what we don’t know and move quickly to close those gaps.

r001.rationale: The response says graphics and AI share underlying computation and transferable engineering skills, but it does not identify mathematical overlap as a reason graphics researchers can learn AI quickly.
